content: Lichen simplex chronicus is a dermatological condition characterized by persistent itching and scratching. This condition often results in a cycle where itching leads to scratching, which in turn exacerbates the itching. The symptoms of lichen simplex chronicus include intense and chronic itching, which may worsen with stress or nervous tension. The affected skin areas often develop thickened, leathery patches due to repeated scratching, a process known as lichenification. These areas may appear hyperpigmented (darker) or reddened, with exaggerated skin lines and distinct borders. Commonly affected sites include the ankles, wrists, neck, anal region, forearms, thighs, lower legs, the back of the knees, and the inner elbows. Additional symptoms may include raw areas, scratch marks, scaling, and plaques. The condition may be triggered by factors such as eczema (atopic dermatitis), psoriasis, or psychological conditions like anxiety, depression, or other emotional stressors. It is particularly common in children who have difficulty refraining from scratching itchy skin conditions or insect bites, as well as in those with repetitive behaviors. Diagnosis is primarily clinical, based on the appearance of the skin and a history of chronic itching and scratching. In some cases, a skin biopsy may be performed to confirm the diagnosis. Urgent medical care should be sought if symptoms worsen, new symptoms develop, or signs of skin infection appear, such as pain, redness, drainage, or fever. Treatment focuses on breaking the itch-scratch cycle. This may involve counseling to emphasize the importance of avoiding scratching, stress management, and behavioral modification. Topical treatments, such as steroid creams or lotions, can help reduce inflammation and itching. Thickened lesions may benefit from peeling ointments containing salicylic acid. Coal tar-based soaps or lotions may also be recommended. Moisturizing and protective dressings, with or without medicated creams, can be applied and left in place for extended periods to aid healing. In some cases, antihistamines, sedatives, or tranquilizers may be prescribed to alleviate itching and stress. Steroid injections directly into the lesions can also help reduce inflammation and itching. For patients with an emotional component to their condition, antidepressants or tranquilizers may be necessary. The prognosis for lichen simplex chronicus is generally favorable with proper management. Reducing stress and avoiding scratching are key to controlling the condition. However, it may recur or manifest in different areas of the body over time.
